info.name: Open Life Requirements API (AU)
info.description:
A vendor-neutral contract for retrieving outstanding underwriting requirements on Australian life applications.

Set `baseUrl` and `accessToken` in the collection variables before sending. The default `baseUrl` points at this contract's local mock — `npm run mock` serves it on port 4012. Request bodies, where an operation takes one, are the contract's own worked examples: validated against the schema and posted at a live mock in CI, so they are known to be accepted.

variable.description: An implementation's base URL. Defaults to this contract's local mock (`npm run mock`, port 4012) so the collection is usable before you have an insurer endpoint.
OAuth2 client-credentials access token. The mock accepts any non-empty value.

header.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response.

query.description: Restrict the snapshot to these adviser codes. Repeat the parameter for several. Omitted, the snapshot covers every code the credential can see, which is the normal case.
Restrict to these requirement categories. Repeat for several. Omitted, every category is returned.
OPTIONAL. Restrict to cases carrying at least one requirement due on or before this date — the triage a consumer wants when the list is longer than the day allows.
OPTIONAL, and only where `capabilities.incremental.supported` is true. Return cases changed since this instant instead of everything outstanding.

Continue an in-progress walk. Supply the `snapshot_id` from the first page alongside the cursor, so the server can prove the cursor belongs to the snapshot the consumer thinks it is walking and reject it with `409` if the snapshot has since expired or been rebuilt.
Continuation token from the previous page's `page.next_cursor`.
Maximum cases per page. A server MAY return fewer; completion is signalled by `complete` and the absence of `page.next_cursor`, never by a short page.

request.description:
Return every application the calling credential can see that is waiting on something, as a consistent snapshot, paged.
This is the contract's primary operation and for most consumers the only one they will call. Walk every page, reconcile against what you hold, and act on what is outstanding.
### The snapshot is the required path, and this is the domain where that matters most
Insurers communicate requirements as notices — an item is raised, and *sometimes* a second message says it arrived. A consumer assembled from those notices holds a list only as good as the messages it never missed, with nothing in the stream to say whether it missed one. Several sources carry no receipt signal at all, so no safe closing rule exists from them and items stay open until a human clears them by hand. Lists built that way only grow, and end up reconciled by telephone.
A complete outstanding-requirements snapshot removes the whole problem. Everything in it is outstanding; anything absent is done with.
### Reconciling on absence — read this before you do it
A case in the last complete snapshot and absent from this one has nothing outstanding. A requirement absent from a case still present has been met or withdrawn. Both are only safe once the **entire** walk has completed, so before acting on absence a consumer MUST have:
- reached a page with `complete: true`; - seen the same `snapshot_id` on every page; and - assembled `total_count` distinct cases.
If any of those fails, treat the run as failed and keep the previous state. A stale worklist is recoverable; one that has closed a book's outstanding requirements is not.
### Scope
Absence means "nothing outstanding" only within `coverage`. A snapshot filtered to two adviser codes says nothing about a third, and one filtered to `medical` says nothing about an outstanding signature.
### Personal information
Responses carry each life's name, date of birth and contact details, because a requirement nobody can attribute or chase is not actionable. Servers MUST send `Cache-Control: no-store`.

header.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response.

request.description:
Return a single application by the insurer's own reference.
Not part of the scheduled pull — a consumer reconciling a book uses the snapshot. This exists for the case an adviser is looking at one client and wants the insurer's current position rather than whatever last night's run captured, which on a case being actively chased is often already out of date.
Also the way to resolve the one ambiguity in the snapshot's absence rule. A case that has dropped out has nothing outstanding, but the snapshot cannot say whether that is because the requirements were met or because the application was declined or withdrawn. Where that distinction matters, read `status` here.
Returns `404` where the case is outside the credential's scope as well as where it does not exist. The two are deliberately indistinguishable: answering `403` for a case that exists but belongs to another practice would confirm its existence to a caller with no right to know.
Carries personal information, so servers MUST send `Cache-Control: no-store`.

header.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response.

request.description:
Describe which parts of a requirement this insurer populates, which categories it reports, how long a snapshot stays walkable, and whether incremental pulls or pushed events are available.
Worth calling before the first snapshot and caching thereafter. Two blocks in particular change how a consumer should behave rather than merely what it displays: `snapshot.categories_available` says which categories may be reconciled on absence at all, and `fields.requirement_type_mapping` says whether this insurer's requirements can be counted alongside another's or only read.
